Second, the ayah closes off every alternative: **"And they will not find, besides Allah, for themselves any protector (*walī*) or any helper (*naṣīr*)."** Ibn Kathir's summary is quietly devastating: **"they have no one else except Allah to respond to their cries."**

So the men slipping away to their houses were running from the only shelter there is, into houses that shelter nothing.

## The portrait, drawn from the inside (18–20)

Having closed the argument, the passage turns to exposure — and it begins with knowledge, not accusation.

**"Allah already knows those among you who keep back (men) from fighting, and those who say to their brethren, 'Come here towards us,' while they come not to the battle except a little."**

Ibn Kathir says Allah's knowledge **encompasses** those who sought to tell others not to go out. Whatever was said quietly between friends had already been heard. The Qur'an's term for them is *al-muʿawwiqīn* — the ones who hold others back, who discourage others from going out.

And the line they used is preserved: ***halumma ilaynā***, "Come here towards us." Ibn Kathir explains that "their brethren" means **their companions, friends and acquaintances**, and that the invitation meant: come to where we are, **in the shade, enjoying fruits.** That single image does more work than any argument. The pull away from duty is rarely a philosophy; it is usually shade and fruit — comfort, offered by someone you know, in a friendly voice.

**"Being miserly towards you"** (*ashiḥḥatan ʿalaykum*). Ibn Kathir gives the broad sense: **"they are mean and have no love or mercy towards you."** As-Suddi reads it more specifically — the stinginess is **with the war booty**. Both readings are preserved in the commentary; the classical scholars did not restrict the word to one meaning.

**"Then when fear comes, you will see them looking to you, their eyes revolving like one over whom hovers death."** This is the most physical line in the passage — the eyes rolling like a man in the throes of death. Ibn Kathir's comment is simply that this is from the intensity of their fear and terror; **this is how afraid these cowards are of fighting.** The Qur'an does not describe their reasoning. It describes their eyes, because at that moment their eyes were more honest than their words.

**"But when the fear departs, they will smite you with sharp tongues."** Ibn Kathir: when security is restored, they speak eloquently and nicely, **claiming that they were the bravest and most chivalrous of men — but they are lying.** Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) glossed *salaqūkum*, "they will smite you," as **"they will start to talk about you."**

Qatādah's description of what follows is worth quoting in full, because it completes the cycle: "But when it comes to the booty, the most miserly of people and the worst to have to share the booty with are those who say, 'Give us, give us, we were there with you' — but during battle they were the most cowardly and the most likely to fail to support the truth."

Absent when it cost. Loudest when it paid.

**"Miserly towards good."** Ibn Kathir reads this as meaning **there is no goodness in them at all**, for they have combined cowardice with lies and little good.

Hence the verdict: **"Such have not believed. Therefore Allah makes their deeds fruitless, and that is ever easy for Allah."** Whatever they had outwardly performed alongside the Muslims is made fruitless — and the closing phrase removes any sense that this is a hard or extraordinary act: it is *ever easy for Allah*.

Then ayah 20 shows the same character after the danger has passed. **"They think that the Confederates have not yet withdrawn."** The siege has lifted; the enemy alliance has gone. But Ibn Kathir explains their state: they imagine the Confederates **are still close by and will return.** He introduces the whole ayah as another aspect of their cowardice and fear — fear that had become their weather, independent of the facts.

**"And if the Confederates should come, they would wish they were in the deserts among the bedouins, seeking news about you."** Ibn Kathir unpacks the wish: if the armies came back, they hope they will **not be present with you in Al-Madinah**, but out in the desert among the nomads, asking after news — *what happened to you with your enemy?* Spectators of the community's fate rather than participants in it. Close enough to hear the outcome; far enough to be safe from it.

**"And if they were to be among you, they would not fight but little."** Ibn Kathir: even physically present, they would not fight alongside you very much, because they are so cowardly and weak, and have so little faith. And then he closes with a restraint worth learning from: **"but Allah knows best about them."**

## Living it

The passage is about a siege, but its logic reaches every fear.

**Flight is not a strategy.** Ayah 16 does not deny that death is frightening. It denies that running changes the appointment. Whatever you are avoiding out of fear — the hard duty, the necessary stand — the avoidance does not extend your life by an hour, and Ibn Kathir warns it may shorten it.

**Your protection was never in the arrangement.** Ayah 17 relocates security from circumstances to Allah. A believer still takes precautions, but knows that walls, plans and allies are not the actual shield — and that if Allah wills mercy for you, nothing on earth can intercept it.

**Watch what you invite others toward.** Ayah 18 exposes not only the man who stays behind but the man who says *halumma ilaynā*, "come over here to us," to his friends. Each of us exerts an ordinary gravitational pull on the people around us — toward the shade and the fruit, or toward the harder and better thing.

**Beware the tongue that arrives after the danger has left.** Ayah 19 shows the man who is invisible during the difficulty and eloquent afterwards, claiming credit and quarrelling over the share. Ibn ʿAbbās read *salaqūkum* as talking about people; Qatādah described the "give us, give us, we were there with you" that follows a victory. The test of a claim is where the claimant was when it was expensive.

**Fear outlives its cause unless it is anchored.** Ayah 20 shows men still bracing for an army that has already gone. Fear untethered from trust in Allah does not end when the danger ends.

**And notice the mercy hidden in ayah 17.** The ayah that shuts every escape route also names Allah's mercy as something no one can withhold from you. To a frightened believer, that is not a threat but the ground to stand on: the only One you cannot escape is the only One who can help you.

passages.title: The believers' response and Allah's reward
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer the ayat just before them. Madinah is under siege by the Confederates, and the surah has just exposed how the hypocrites reacted — with sneering, excuses and flight. Now Allah turns to the believers: here is the man you should have been watching (ayah 21), here is what faith says when the armies come into view (ayah 22), here are the men who kept their word to the end (ayah 23), here is why Allah puts people through such a night (ayah 24), and here is how it ended, with Allah Himself dispersing the enemy (ayah 25). One contrast holds the passage together: **broken covenants against kept ones**, and Allah's verdict on both.

## The scene these ayat are answering

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets it out plainly. When the allied armies encircled the city, the hypocrites began saying that "Allah and His Messenger did not promise us but deceitfully" (ayah 12) — an inner disbelief finally breaking the surface. Two groups of them were part of the defence outwardly only. One called out, "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you to stay; so go back" (ayah 13). The other went to the Prophet ﷺ asking leave to withdraw on false excuses, pleading, "In fact our homes are vulnerable" — and the Qurʼān answers that they were not vulnerable at all: "They wanted nothing but to escape" (ayah 13).

Then, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the text turns to the sincere believers and praises their firmness and fortitude. So read ayah 21 not as a detached maxim but as a rebuke and a rescue delivered mid-siege — Ibn Kathir is explicit that Allah is addressing "those who were anxious and impatient and were shaken by feelings of panic on the day of Al-Ahzab."

## Ayah 21: "In the Messenger of Allah you have a good example"

**A principle, not a compliment.** Ibn Kathir calls this ayah "an important principle": to follow the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in all his words and deeds. The word rendered "example" is *uswah* — a pattern you place your own life against, a model to be copied rather than merely admired. And the sense of the ayah, Ibn Kathir says, is a question aimed straight at the panicking: *"why do you not take him ﷺ as an example and follow his lead?"*

**Copied in what, exactly?** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah commanded people to take the Prophet ﷺ as their model on the day of al-Aḥzāb specifically "with regard to patience, guarding, striving and waiting for Allah to provide the way out."

**Who can actually take him as a model.** It is a good example "for him who hopes in Allah and the Last Day, and remembers Allah much." Three things qualify a heart to follow him under pressure: hope in Allah, a live expectation of the Hereafter, and abundant *dhikr* (remembrance of Allah). Without those, the example is visible but not imitable — a man who does not expect to meet Allah has no reason to hold a trench when fleeing is easier.

**How far does "follow him" extend?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this comes "almost in the form of a legal rule of conduct," and that from here it stands proved that all the sayings and doings of the Prophet ﷺ are to be followed. But it also records the scholars' calibration of the *degree* of following. The rule the Sharīʿah authorities give: an act or omission of the Prophet ﷺ proved to have been done **as an obligation** must be obeyed and followed as *wājib* — binding. An act or omission proved to have been done as **preferable conduct** (*istiḥbāb*) rather than as an obligation is to be followed as *mustaḥabb* — commendable, but not a necessary obligation, which means that going against it is not declared a sin. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the reader to al-Jaṣṣāṣ's *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān* for the detailed discussion.

## Ayah 22: what faith says when it sees the armies

Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah by saying that Allah now tells us about His believing servants who believed Allah's promise to them, and how He will make the consequences good for them in this world and in the Hereafter. The believers looked out at the massed Confederates and said: *"This is what Allah and His Messenger had promised us; and Allah and His Messenger had spoken the truth."*

**What promise did they mean?** Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah — both cited by Ibn Kathir — said they meant Allah's words in Sūrat al-Baqarah: "Or think you that you will enter Paradise without such trials as came to those who passed away before you? They were afflicted with severe poverty and ailments and were so shaken that even the Messenger and those who believed along with him said, 'When will come the help of Allah?' Yes! Certainly, the help of Allah is near!" (2:214). Their meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, was: *this is the trial and test that Allah and His Messenger promised us would be followed by the help and victory of Allah that is near.*

The very sight that broke the hypocrites was to the believers **evidence that the promise was true**: they had been told the road to Paradise runs through exactly this. The armies on the horizon were not a refutation of the promise; they were the promise arriving on schedule. That is why one scene produced two opposite sentences: "Allah and His Messenger did not promise us but deceitfully" (ayah 12), and "Allah and His Messenger had spoken the truth" (ayah 22).

**"It only added to their faith and to their submissiveness."** Ibn Kathir explains: "it only added" means at that time of stress and difficulty; "to their faith" means faith in Allah; and "to their submissiveness" (*taslīm*) means their submission to His commands and their obedience to His Messenger ﷺ.

He then draws a doctrinal point from the phrase: this indicates that faith can increase and strengthen in accordance with people's circumstances — "as the majority of scholars stated: faith can increase and decrease," and he notes that he has treated the question at the beginning of his commentary on al-Bukhārī. So *īmān* is not a fixed quantity you either hold or lose. Hardship is one of the things that grows it — in a heart already turned toward Allah.

## Ayah 23: "men who have been true to what they pledged"

Ibn Kathir frames this ayah as the mirror-image of what came before: when Allah mentions how the hypocrites broke their promise to Him that they would not turn their backs, He describes the believers as firmly adhering to their covenant and their promise. The hypocrites had said "Truly, our homes lie open" — "and they lay not open. They but wished to flee" (33:13) — though "indeed they had already made a covenant with Allah not to turn their backs" (33:15). Ayah 23 is the honour roll set against that record.

**The word *naḥbah*.** The ayah says some of them "have fulfilled their *naḥbah*" — a word the early authorities read in more than one way, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference rather than flattening it:

- **"Met their appointed time"** — that is, death. This is how "some of them" read it.
- **"Their covenant"** — al-Bukhārī's reading, which, as he says, refers the word back to the beginning of the ayah ("true to what they pledged to Allah"). **Mujāhid** said the same: *naḥbah* = their covenant.
- **A vow** — "some of them said that the word *naḥbah* means a vow."
- **al-Ḥasan** drew the senses together: "They died true to their covenant and loyal, and some are still waiting to die in a similar manner, and some of them have never changed in the least." Ibn Kathir adds that this was also the view of **Qatādah** and **Ibn Zayd**.

And "some of them are still waiting" — **Mujāhid** explains: they are waiting for battle so that they can do well. Not waiting passively; waiting for their turn to give what the others already gave.

**"But they have never changed in the least."** Ibn Kathir: they never changed their covenant or were disloyal or committed treachery, "but they persisted in what they had promised and did not break their vow" — unlike the hypocrites of ayah 13.

### The man behind the ayah: Anas bin an-Naḍr

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Anas bin Mālik said: "We think that this ayah was revealed concerning Anas bin an-Naḍr." Ibn Kathir notes that this particular report was reported only by al-Bukhārī, but that there are corroborating reports with other chains of narration.

Imam Ahmad recorded the fuller story from Anas bin Mālik. His paternal uncle Anas bin an-Naḍr, after whom he was named, was not present with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Badr, and this distressed him. He said: *"The first battle at which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was present, and I was absent; if Allah shows me another battle with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Allah will see what I will do!"* — and, the narration adds, he did not want to say more than that.

He was present with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Uḥud, where he met Saʿd bin Muʿādh. He said to him, "O Abū ʿAmr! Where are you going?" The reply came: *"I long for the fragrance of Paradise and I have found it near the mountain of Uḥud."* He fought them until he was killed. Eighty-odd stab wounds and spear wounds were found on his body, and his sister — Anas's paternal aunt, ar-Rabayyiʿ bint an-Naḍr — said, *"I only recognised my brother by his fingertips."* Then this ayah was revealed. "They used to think," the narration ends, "that it had been revealed concerning him and his companions." Ibn Kathir notes that this narration was also recorded by Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī.

That is what "true to what they pledged" looks like in one life: a word given, said once and no more, then paid beyond any possibility of retreat.

**One man named by the Prophet ﷺ himself.** Ibn Jarīr narrated from Mūsā bin Ṭalḥah that Muʿāwiyah bin Abī Sufyān stood up and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: *'Ṭalḥah is one of those who have fulfilled their naḥbah.'*" So the first half of the ayah — those who have *fulfilled* — is not left as an abstraction: the Prophet ﷺ placed a named Companion inside it.

**A footnote that is really a testimony.** Al-Bukhārī recorded that Zayd bin Thābit said: when the Muṣḥaf was being written down, an ayah of Sūrat al-Aḥzāb was missing which he used to hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting — and he did not find it with anyone except Khuzaymah bin Thābit al-Anṣārī, whose testimony the Messenger of Allah ﷺ counted as equal to that of two other men. The ayah was this one. Ibn Kathir notes that it was recorded by al-Bukhārī but not by Muslim, also by Ahmad in his *Musnad*, and by at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī in the chapters on tafsir in their *Sunans*; at-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." The ayah praising men whose word could be relied on was itself secured through a man whose word the Prophet ﷺ had declared worth two.

## Ayah 24: why Allah stages such a night

"That Allah may reward the men of truth for their truth, and punish the hypocrites, if He wills, or accept their repentance by turning to them. Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."

**The purpose of the trial.** Ibn Kathir: Allah tests His servants with fear and shaking "so as to tell the evil from the good, as each will be known by his deeds." He then handles the obvious theological question head-on: although Allah knows what the outcome will be before anything happens, He does not punish anyone on the basis of His knowledge until they actually do what He knows they will do. He cites "And surely, We shall try you till We test those who strive hard and patient, and We shall test your facts" (47:31) — noting that this refers to knowing something *after* it happens, even though Allah knows it before it comes to pass — and "Allah will not leave the believers in the state in which you are now, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good" (3:179). The siege did not inform Allah of anything. It made visible, in deeds, what was already true in hearts.

**Rewarded for what.** "That Allah may reward the men of truth for their truth" means, Ibn Kathir says, for their patience in adhering to the covenant they had made with Allah and keeping their promise. Truthfulness here is not accuracy of speech but fidelity of action: a word given and then honoured.

**The door left open.** The hypocrites "are the ones who broke the covenant and went against the commands of Allah, for which they deserve to be punished" — but Ibn Kathir stresses that in this world they remain subject to His will: if He wills, He will leave them as they are until they meet Him and He punishes them; if He wills, He will guide them to give up their hypocrisy and to believe and do righteous deeds after they had been wrongdoers and sinners. And the ayah closes not on the threat but on the mercy: "Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" — because, as Ibn Kathir says, His mercy and kindness towards His creation prevail over His wrath.

## Ayah 25: driven back in their rage, gaining nothing

"And Allah drove back those who disbelieved in their rage: they gained no advantage. Allah sufficed for the believers in the fighting. And Allah is Ever All-Strong, All-Mighty."

**How the siege broke.** Ibn Kathir: Allah drove the Confederates away from Madinah by sending against them a wind and troops of angels. He adds a striking observation — had Allah not made His Messenger ﷺ a mercy to the worlds, that wind would have been more severe than the barren wind sent against ʿĀd; but Allah has said, "And Allah would not punish them while you are amongst them" (8:33). Even the enemy was shielded by the presence of the Prophet ﷺ among them.

**Why a wind, of all things.** They had gathered on the basis of their whims, and they were, Ibn Kathir notes, "a mixture of tribes and parties with a variety of opinions" — so it was befitting that a wind should be sent against them that would scatter them and break up their gathering, driving them back disappointed and lost in their hatred and enmity.

**"They gained no advantage."** They did not achieve any worldly good — the victory and booty they had hoped for — nor any good in the Hereafter, because of their sin of declaring enmity against the Messenger ﷺ and seeking to kill him and destroy his army. Ibn Kathir adds a sobering principle: whoever wants and seriously intends to do a thing is the same as one who actually does it. Their intention was itself their record.

**"Allah sufficed for the believers in the fighting."** Ibn Kathir: they did not have to fight them in order to expel them from their land — Allah Alone sufficed them, helped His servant and granted victory to His troops. Hence, he says, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: *"None has the right to be worshipped but Allah, Alone; He was true to His promise, and He helped His servant, and He gave might to His soldiers, and defeated the Confederates alone, and there is nothing after Him."* Ibn Kathir reports this from a hadith of Abū Hurayrah.

And in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs it is recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin Abī Awfā said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked Allah against the Confederates and said: *"O Allah, Who revealed the Book and is swift in bringing to account, defeat the Confederates; O Allah, defeat them and shake them."* The model of patience in ayah 21 was, at the same time, the man on his knees asking.

**The turning point.** Ibn Kathir reads "Allah sufficed for the believers in the fighting" as indicating that there would be a cessation of war between the Muslims and Quraysh: after this the idolaters did not attack the Muslims; on the contrary, the Muslims attacked them in their own land. Imam Ahmad recorded that Sulaymān bin Ṣurad said that on the day of al-Aḥzāb the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Now we will attack them and they will not attack us."* Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhārī also recorded this in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*.

**"Ever All-Strong, All-Mighty."** Ibn Kathir: by His power and might He drove them back disappointed and lost; they did not achieve anything; Allah granted victory to Islam and its followers, fulfilled His promise, and helped His servant and Messenger.

## Living it

**Take the Prophet ﷺ as your working model, not your distant hero.** Copy him where the sources say to copy him here: patience, guarding, striving, and waiting for Allah to provide the way out — keeping in view the scholars' distinction between what he did as an obligation and what he did as preferable conduct.

**Read hardship as the promise arriving, not the promise failing.** The believers of ayah 22 had a verse ready in their hearts (2:214), and it reframed the whole horizon. The hypocrites had none, so the same scene read to them as betrayal.

**Let your word to Allah be something you actually pay.** Anas bin an-Naḍr said what he would do if Allah gave him another battle, and did not want to say more than that — then he did it. Ayah 23 honours those who did not *change*, and equally those "still waiting" for their moment, provided they have not altered.

**Do not slam the door Allah left open.** Ayah 24 names the hypocrites and still suspends their fate on His will, closing on forgiveness and mercy.

passages.title: The betraying tribe brought down from their strongholds
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close the account of the Battle of the Trench by telling what happened *after* the siege lifted — not to the Confederate armies who were driven back, but to the tribe inside Madinah that had broken its treaty while the city was surrounded. Ayah 26 describes how Allah brought them down from their fortresses and cast terror into their hearts; ayah 27 turns that single local outcome into a promise stretching far beyond Madinah. What holds the two together is one theme: Allah alone reversed the situation, and what looked like the Muslims' most dangerous moment became the doorway to everything that came after.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the flow that leads here. Earlier in the sūrah, when the siege was at its worst, the hypocrites and "those having malady in their hearts" were saying that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ had promised them nothing but deception (ayah 12). Two groups of them are then described: one that broke and ran without permission, calling out "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you to stay, so go back" (ayah 13), and another that asked the Prophet ﷺ for leave on the excuse that their homes were exposed — an excuse the Qur'an exposes as false, since "they wanted nothing but to escape" (ayah 13). Against that, the sincere believers are praised for their firmness and fortitude, and in ayah 21 comes the great statement that in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ there is a good model to follow.

So by the time we reach ayat 25–27, the Qur'an has already sorted the community by what the siege revealed about each heart. These closing ayat show what Allah then did — and they answer the hypocrites' jeer about deceptive promises with hard facts on the ground.

## The betrayal that made this necessary

Ibn Kathir gives the background. When the Confederates came and camped outside Madinah, Banū Qurayẓah broke the covenant that existed between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This came about through Ḥuyayy bin Akhṭab an-Naḍarī, who entered their stronghold and would not leave their leader Kaʿb bin Asad alone until he agreed to break the covenant. Among the things Ḥuyayy said to him was: "Woe to you! This is the opportunity for glory. The Quraysh and their company of men from various tribes, and the Ghaṭafān and their followers, have come to you, and they will stay here until they eliminate Muhammad and his companions."

Kaʿb's reply is worth sitting with, because he saw clearly and acted against what he saw: "No, by Allah, this is the opportunity for humiliation. Woe to you, O Ḥuyayy, you are a bad omen. Leave us alone." But Ḥuyayy kept trying to persuade him until he agreed — laying down the condition that if the Confederates went away without doing anything, Ḥuyayy would join them in their stronghold and share their fate.

When news of the broken covenant reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he and the Muslims were very distressed by it — the city was besieged from outside, and now its inner flank was open. Then Allah helped him by suppressing his enemy and driving them back disappointed and lost, having gained nothing, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah in triumph. The people put down their weapons.

## "But the angels have not put down their weapons"

Ibn Kathir describes what happened next. While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was washing off the dust of battle in the house of Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her), Jibrīl (upon him be peace) came to him wearing a turban of brocade, riding on a mule on which was a cloth of silk brocade, and said, "Have you put down your weapons, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said, "Yes." Jibrīl said, "But the angels have not put down their weapons. I have just now come back from pursuing the people." Then he said that Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, commands him to get up and go to Banū Qurayẓah. According to another report, Jibrīl said, "What a fighter you are! Have you put down your weapons?" — and when the Prophet ﷺ asked where he should go, said, "Banū Qurayẓah, for Allah has commanded me to shake them."

That is the hinge of ayah 26. The word Allah uses is **وَأَنزَلَ** — *and He brought down*. Not "you brought them down." The march was human; the bringing-down was divine, and Jibrīl's words show the unseen army was still in motion before the human one had set out.

## The march

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ got up immediately and commanded the people to march towards Banū Qurayẓah, who were a few miles from Madinah. This was after Ẓuhr, and he ﷺ said that no one among them should pray ʿAṣr except at Banū Qurayẓah. (Ibn Kathir gives these words of the Prophet ﷺ without naming a ḥadīth collection, so they are passed on here exactly as his commentary gives them, and no collection is attached to them.)

The people set out, and the time for the prayer came while they were still on the road. Some of them prayed on the road, saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had only wanted to make them march quickly. Others said they would not pray it until they reached Banū Qurayẓah. Ibn Kathir then records one sentence, and it is worth reading exactly as he wrote it: **"Neither of the two groups were rebuked for what they did."**

He ﷺ left Ibn Umm Maktūm (may Allah be pleased with him) in charge of Madinah, and had given the flag to ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him). Then he went to Banū Qurayẓah and laid siege to them for twenty-five days.

## Saʿd bin Muʿādh and the judgement

When this had gone on for too long, they agreed to accept the judgement of Saʿd bin Muʿādh, the leader of the Aws — because the Aws had been their allies during the Jāhiliyyah, so they thought he would treat them kindly, as ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy bin Salūl had done for his allies of Banū Qaynuqāʿ when he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to set them free.

What they did not know was that Saʿd had been struck by an arrow in his medial arm vein during the campaign of al-Khandaq. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had had the vein cauterised and had brought him to stay in a tent in the Masjid so that he could keep a close eye on him. One of the things Saʿd (may Allah be pleased with him) said in his supplication was: "O Allah, if there is still anything that has to do with the war against Quraysh, then keep me alive for it, and if You decree that the war between us and them is over, then let the bleeding be renewed, but do not let me die until I get my satisfaction with regard to Banū Qurayẓah." Ibn Kathir says plainly that Allah answered his prayer and decreed that they would agree to be referred to him for judgement — and that this was their own free choice. That is worth pausing on: the request of one believer lying wounded in a tent shaped how the whole affair ended, and the people it concerned walked into it by their own decision.

Saʿd was called from Madinah to pass judgement, and arrived riding on a donkey that had been specially equipped for him. Some of the Aws began to urge him not to be too harsh — "O Saʿd, they are your clients so be kind to them" — trying to soften his heart. But he kept quiet and did not answer them. When they persisted, he said: "Now it is time for Saʿd to make sure that no rebuke or censure will divert him from the path of Allah." Then they knew that he would not let them live.

When he reached the tent where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Stand up for your leader (*sayyidikum*)." So the Muslims stood up for him and welcomed him with honour and respect — Ibn Kathir explains this was as befitted his status and so that his judgement would have more impact. When he sat down, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, pointing to them, that these people had agreed to accept his judgement, so let him pass judgement on them as he wished.

Saʿd said that his judgement would be carried out; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Yes." And on those who are in this tent? "Yes." And on those who are on this side — pointing towards the side where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was, but not looking directly at him out of respect for him? "Yes."

Then he gave it: "My judgement is that their fighters should be killed and their children and wealth should be seized." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that he had judged according to the ruling of Allah from above the seven heavens; according to another report, that he had judged according to the ruling of the Sovereign (الملك). (Again, Ibn Kathir gives these words without naming a ḥadīth collection.)

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that ditches should be dug, and the fighters were brought tied by their shoulders and were beheaded — there were between seven hundred and eight hundred of them. The children who had not yet reached adolescence, and the women, were taken prisoner, and their wealth was seized. Ibn Kathir notes that he set all of this out both briefly and in detail, with evidence and ḥadīths, in the book of Sīrah he had written.

**From the Sunnah.** Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAṭiyah al-Quraẓī said: "I was shown to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Qurayẓah, because they were not sure about me. The Prophet ﷺ told them to look at me to see whether I had grown any body hair yet. They looked and saw that I had not grown any body hair, so they let me go and I was put with the other prisoners." Ibn Kathir adds that this was also recorded by the Sunan compilers, that at-Tirmidhī said it is *Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ*, and that an-Nasāʾī also recorded something similar from ʿAṭiyah. The report matters for two reasons: it shows the judgement fell on *fighters*, with physical maturity as the line, and it shows that individuals were checked one by one rather than swept together.

## Opening the words of ayah 26

**ظَاهَرُوهُم — "those who backed them."** Ibn Kathir explains this as those who helped and supported them in their war against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The charge named in the ayah is that concrete act of backing — supporting an army that had come against the city they were bound by covenant to keep faith with.

**مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ — "of the People of the Scripture."** This means Banū Qurayẓah, who were Jews from one of the tribes of Israel. Ibn Kathir adds a detail full of sorrow: their forefathers had settled in the Ḥijāz long ago, seeking to follow the Unlettered Prophet of whom they read in the Tawrāh and Injīl. They had come to the right place — and then, as Allah says, "when there came to them that which they had recognised, they disbelieved in it" (2:89).

**مِن صَيَاصِيهِمْ — "from their forts."** Ibn Kathir reports that this means from their strongholds, and that this was the view of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others of the Salaf. The image is deliberate: high, thick-walled places built for exactly this situation. And it is Allah who *brought them down* from them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the mechanism plainly — by putting the awe of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and his Muslim followers into their hearts, Allah made them come down from their strong fortresses.

**وَقَذَفَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الرُّعْبَ — "and cast terror into their hearts."** Ibn Kathir glosses this as fear, and gives the reason: they had supported the idolaters in their war against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "and the one who knows is not like the one who does not know." They had terrified the Muslims and intended to kill them so as to gain earthly power, but their plans backfired: the idolaters ran away and the believers were victorious while the disbelievers were losers; where they had aimed for glory, they were humiliated; they wanted to eradicate the Muslims but were themselves eradicated — and in addition to all this they are doomed in the Hereafter, so by all accounts they are counted as losers. Read that against Kaʿb bin Asad's own warning to Ḥuyayy — "this is the opportunity for humiliation" — and you see a man who named the outcome in advance and went along with it anyway.

**فَرِيقًا تَقْتُلُونَ وَتَأْسِرُونَ فَرِيقًا — "a group you killed, and a group you made captives."** Ibn Kathir: those who were killed were their warriors, and the prisoners were their children and women. Note the shift in who acts — Allah brought them down and cast the terror; the taking is spoken of as yours. Human effort was real, but it operated inside a work that was already Allah's.

## Ayah 27: from Madinah to lands not yet trodden

**وَأَوْرَثَكُمْ أَرْضَهُمْ وَدِيَارَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ — "and He caused you to inherit their lands, and their houses, and their riches."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short: "He gave these things to you after you killed them." The verb is one of *inheritance* — the wording keeps the transfer in Allah's hands, as an estate assigned rather than a prize grabbed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the same phrase as Allah having made the Muslims the inheritors of their properties, homes and areas of concentration.

**وَأَرْضًا لَّمْ تَطَئُوهَا — "and a land which you had not trodden."** Here the ayah steps out of Madinah entirely. Ibn Kathir reports that it was said this was Khaybar, or that it was the lands of the Persians and Romans; Ibn Jarīr said it could be that all of these are referred to. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as good news of future victories: gone is the time when the disbelievers attacked, and now the cycle of Muslim victories will begin, reaching lands their feet have not touched yet. And this prophecy unfolded itself during the tenure of the noble Ṣaḥābah, when everyone witnessed the spectacle of the great empires ruled by Cyrus and Caesar come under them.

Feel the scale of that sentence. It was given to a community that had just come through the campaign of al-Khandaq and the affair of one tribe a few miles from home — and it speaks to them about ground they have never walked on.

**وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرًا — "and Allah is able to do all things."** The closing seal. It is what makes the promise of unvisited land credible: the same Power that cast terror into fortified hearts can hand over empires. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends the passage: and Allah does what He wills.

## Living it

**Allah's promise is answered in events, not arguments.** The hypocrites had said in ayah 12 that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ promised nothing but deception. Ayat 26–27 do not debate them; they report what happened, and then extend the promise further.

**Read the outcome, not the odds.** Banū Qurayẓah calculated in the moment the Confederates looked unbeatable. Ḥuyayy called it "the opportunity for glory." It ended, as Ibn Kathir sums up, in the reverse of everything they were reaching for.

**Hold Ibn Kathir's one sentence lightly and carefully.** Two groups of Companions, one command about ʿAṣr, two readings — and all he tells us is that neither group was rebuked. He does not explain it further, and neither will we; but that restraint is worth carrying into our own disagreements with people who are trying, as we are, to obey.

**Say what is right even when the room is pulling at you.** Saʿd bin Muʿādh, wounded, surrounded by his own tribe urging him to soften: "Now it is time for Saʿd to make sure that no rebuke or censure will divert him from the path of Allah."

**Ask.** A man lying in a tent in the Masjid asked Allah not to let him die until this matter was settled — and Ibn Kathir tells us Allah answered his prayer, and arranged it through the free choice of the very people concerned. He is able to do all things.

passages.title: The Prophet's wives offered a choice
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the moment Allah told His Messenger ﷺ to lay a choice before his wives: the comfort and ornament of this world, with an honourable release — or Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the Home of the Hereafter, on the hard terms life in his household actually offered. Ayah 28 puts one option; ayah 29 puts the other. Ma'arif ul Qur'an gives ayah 29 the title **the Verse of Choice**: the verse in which the blessed wives are given the choice either to seek divorce from him, or to remain with him seeking the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

## Why this came down when it did

Ma'arif ul Qur'an sets the passage in the flow of the surah. Out of the objectives of Surah al-Ahzab, it says, the most important is the stress placed on avoiding everything that may cause pain to the Prophet ﷺ, alongside a reiteration of instructions to obey him and seek his pleasure. Just before this, the surah dealt with the battle of al-Ahzab — the pain the disbelievers and hypocrites caused him, their ultimate disgrace, and the praise of sincere believers who sacrificed what they had at his word and were promised high ranks in the Hereafter. Now the address turns inward, to his own home. His wives, Ma'arif says, are particularly taught to be careful that no word or deed issuing from them causes him pain — and this is possible only when they devote themselves and become totally obedient to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

So the choice was not abstract. Ma'arif is explicit that it is limited to one or some incidents that came from the side of the blessed wives — things contrary to the intent of the Prophet ﷺ, which caused him pain.

**The request for a larger allowance.** One of these incidents is reported from Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) and appears in the Sahih of Muslim and elsewhere as well. The wives came together and asked the Prophet ﷺ that their sustenance allowance should be increased. Abu Hayyan, in *Tafsir al-Bahr ul-Muhit*, explains the background: the victories of Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayzah after the battle of al-Ahzab, coupled with the distribution of spoils, had generated a certain improved economic wellbeing among ordinary Muslims. The wives thought the Prophet ﷺ would have set aside a share for himself too. So they appealed to him jointly, saying — as Ma'arif renders it — that the wives of Cyrus and Caesar were laden with all sorts of valuable ornaments and dresses and had maids appointed to serve them, "while you see how hungry and ill-clad we are."

Ma'arif's reading of the Prophet's ﷺ reaction is worth pausing over. Hearing this demand that they be treated on a par with the lifestyles of kings and the worldly-wise rich, he was grieved at how much they had missed appreciating the worth and value of living in the home of a prophet of Allah. And Ma'arif is equally careful about them: on their part, they never thought their submission would cause him pain. It was simply because of the wellbeing of common Muslims around them that they thought of the same for themselves. This is not a story of villains. It is a story of a household being held to a standard higher than the ordinary one.

**A second possible cause.** Ma'arif also notes that, according to some hadith narratives, following the event of the honey drink at the home of Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with her) — dealt with in detail under Surah at-Tahrim 66:1–5 — a situation created by the mutual sense of importance among the blessed wives became the cause of this choice of divorce. Ma'arif does not force a decision: if the two happened close in time to each other, it is not remote to believe both could be the cause. Two considerations nevertheless lean toward the financial request. Abu Hayyan says that the placing of that incident after the battle of al-Ahzab supports the likelihood that this very demand became the cause. And Ma'arif adds that the words of the Verse of Choice are more supportive of that understanding, since the verse itself says: "If you intend the life of this world and its charm."

## The day Abu Bakr and Umar came in

Ibn Kathir preserves the scene at length. Imam Ahmad recorded that Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

> Abu Bakr came to ask permission to see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the people were sitting at his door, and the Prophet ﷺ was sitting, but he did not give him permission. Then Umar came and asked permission to see him, but he did not give him permission. Then he gave Abu Bakr and Umar permission, and they entered. The Prophet ﷺ was sitting with his wives around him, and he was silent.
>
> Umar said, "I will tell the Prophet ﷺ something to make him smile." Umar said, "O Messenger of Allah, if only you had seen the daughter of Zayd — the wife of Umar — asking me to spend on her just now; I broke her neck!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled so broadly that his molars could be seen, and he said: **"They are around me asking me to spend on them."**
>
> Abu Bakr got up to deal with Aishah, and Umar got up to deal with Hafsah, and both of them were saying, "You are asking the Prophet ﷺ for that which he does not have!" But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stopped them, and they (his wives) said, "By Allah, after this we will not ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for anything that he does not have."
>
> Then Allah revealed the ayah telling him to give them the choice, and he started with Aishah. He said: **"I am going to tell you something, and I would like you not to hasten to respond until you consult your parents."** She said, "What is it?" He recited to her: *"O Prophet! Say to your wives…"* Aishah said, "Do I need to consult my parents concerning you? I choose Allah and His Messenger, but I ask you not to tell of my choice to your other wives." He ﷺ said: **"Allah did not send me to be harsh, but He sent me to teach in a gentle and easy manner. If any of them asks me what your decision was, I will tell her."**

Ibn Kathir notes that this narration was also recorded by Muslim, but not by al-Bukhari; an-Nasa'i also recorded it.

There is a great deal in that one report. First, the silence: a house under strain, and a man saying nothing — until a friend's rough joke draws a smile so wide his molars showed. Second, the Prophet ﷺ restrained the two fathers rather than letting them scold their daughters, even in a matter that had grieved him. Third, the wives corrected themselves before the revelation came down. And fourth, his answer to Aishah's request is a window into his whole prophetic manner. He would not conceal the truth of her choice, and he would not use it as leverage over the others. He was not sent to be harsh; he was sent to teach gently, and to make things easy.

## "He started with me"

Al-Bukhari narrated from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to her when Allah commanded him to give his wives the choice. She said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ started with me," and said:

> **"I am going to tell you about something, and you do not have to hasten to respond until you consult your parents."**

Her comment on this is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the tafsir literature: *he knew that my parents would never tell me to leave him.* The Tirmidhi report cited by Ma'arif — which Tirmidhi graded *hasan sahih* (sound and reliable) — has her calling this his special favour to her: he forbade her from expressing an opinion before consulting her parents, because he was certain her parents would never advise her to opt for separation from him.

Then he recited the two ayat. And she did not wait. "Concerning what do I need to consult my parents? I choose Allah and His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter."

Ibn Kathir records that he also narrated this without a chain of narrators, adding her words: **then all the wives of the Prophet ﷺ did the same as I.** The Tirmidhi report in Ma'arif says the same: after her, this command of the Qur'an was announced to all the blessed wives, and all of them said what she had said first — none of them elected worldly affluence over the honour of being the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.

Ikrimah said that at that time he was married to nine women: five from Quraysh — Aishah, Hafsah, Umm Habibah, Sawdah and Umm Salamah; and Safiyyah bint Huyayy an-Nadariyyah, Maymunah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah, Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyyah and Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith al-Mustalaqiyyah (may Allah be pleased with all of them). Nine women, every one of them free to leave with a provision and an honourable release. Nine times the same answer.

## The two desires

The passage is built on a single repeated verb. Ayah 28: *in kuntunna turidna al-hayat ad-dunya wa zinataha* — "if you desire the life of this world and its glitter." Ayah 29: *wa in kuntunna turidna Allaha wa rasulahu wa'd-dar al-akhirah* — "but if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter." Same construction, same verb of wanting, two objects. The Qur'an is not asking what they possess or what they endure. It is asking what they *desire* — where the heart's intention actually points.

The first object is doubled: this life **and its glitter** — the adornment, the visible finery. That is precisely what had been named in the request: ornaments, dresses, servants. The second object is tripled: Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and the Home of the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir reads the alternatives concretely — either they separate from him and go to someone else with whom they can find what they want of the life of this world and its attractions, or they patiently bear the straitened circumstances with the Prophet ﷺ, for which they will have a great reward with Allah.

And note the address in ayah 28: *Ya ayyuha'n-Nabi* — "O Prophet." He is addressed by his office, and then told *qul li-azwajika*, "say to your wives." The message reaches them through him; the choice is delivered by the very man they would be choosing between keeping and leaving.

The closing of ayah 29 names the reward: Allah has prepared **for the doers of good among you an enormous reward**. Ma'arif draws out what the two branches meant in practice. If they took the first option — continuing to live with him in his straitened economic condition — they would deserve greater reward and higher ranks in the Hereafter than other women. If they took the second, they would not have to face the displeasure customary with worldly people; in fact they would be given a send-off with honour, and parting gifts in accordance with the Sunnah. Even the exit was designed to be dignified.

Ibn Kathir adds the ending: they chose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and the Home of the Hereafter — **then Allah gave them the best both of this world and of the Hereafter.** They renounced the world's glitter and were not, in the end, deprived of the world.

## Was it a divorce?

No. Imam Ahmad recorded from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her): "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave us the choice, and we chose him, so giving us that choice was not regarded as divorce." Ibn Kathir notes it was recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim from the hadith of al-A'mash. The offer, unaccepted, left the marriages exactly as they were.

**A point of fiqh where the scholars differed.** Ma'arif explains that the choice of divorce can be given to a woman in two different forms. In the first, the power of divorce is entrusted to the woman: if she wishes, she can divorce herself and become free — and as soon as she opts for it she is divorced, without any act on the part of the husband. In the second, the power of giving divorce remains in the husband's hands, but he promises her that whenever she wishes it, he will divorce her — so divorce is not effected merely by her opting for it unless he pronounces it.

Which of the two was offered here? Ma'arif reports that some commentators held it was the first form, while others maintained it was the second. The esteemed author of *Bayan ul-Qur'an* commented that the verse carries both probabilities, and that until one of the two stands determined on the authority of some definitive text, there is no need to determine any form on one's own. That restraint is itself instructive: where the sources genuinely leave a question open, the scholarly habit is to leave it open rather than manufacture certainty.

## The ruling drawn from ayah 28

Ma'arif derives a general principle from this verse. Where there is no congruity between the temperaments of a married couple, the desirable approach is to give the wife the option: either to live with her husband while being content with whatever state he is in, or else to be allowed to leave honourably according to the Sunnah, with divorce and a gift of pairs of apparel.

But Ma'arif is careful about the *strength* of that ruling: what can be proved from the verse is its desirability only; there is no proof to support its obligation. It notes that some leading Muslim jurists have argued in favour of its obligatory nature, and on that basis have given the wife of a penniless man — one incapable of providing her living expenses — the right to secure a divorce from the court. Ma'arif refers the reader to the full details in *Ahkam ul-Qur'an*, Part V, under this very verse. Both positions are on the table; the tafsir names them rather than flattening them.

## Living it

**Say the hard thing plainly, and leave the other person free.** The Prophet ﷺ did not sulk and did not hint. He put the real choice on the table, offered a provision and an honourable release, and told Aishah not to hasten her answer until she had consulted her parents. Silence and pressure are both easier; neither is what he did here.

**Do not weaponise one person's answer against another.** Asked to keep her choice from the other wives, he answered that Allah did not send him to be harsh, but sent him to teach in a gentle and easy manner — and that if any of them asked, he would tell her. He refused to hide Aishah's choice, and equally refused to hold it over the others.

**Watch what the eye drifts toward.** Ma'arif is clear that the wives never imagined their request would cause him pain; it grew out of the improving circumstances of the Muslims around them. The passage does not paint them as wrongdoers. It asks a sharper question: when the two are laid side by side, which one do you actually *desire*?

**Part well, if you must part.** Even the option to leave carried provision, release in a handsome manner, and parting gifts in accordance with the Sunnah. A marriage that ends need not end in humiliation.

And the ending is the point. Nine women, each free to walk away with a provision and her honour intact, chose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and the Home of the Hereafter — and Allah, as Ibn Kathir says, then gave them the best both of this world and of the Hereafter. May Allah be pleased with them all.

passages.title: The household of the Prophet held to a higher standard
passages.tafsir:
This passage speaks directly to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ — the Mothers of the Believers. Ayat 30–31 announce the doubled scale on which their deeds are weighed, ayat 32–33 give the instructions that follow from that standing, and ayah 34 names the blessing that put them on that scale — that Allah's verses were recited in their houses. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link explicitly: the words of ayah 34 "point out to this reason" for the doubling in ayah 30.

Ibn Kathir describes the addressees as those "who chose Allah and His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter, and remained married to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" — and so, he says, "it was befitting that there should be rulings which applied only to them, and not to other women." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: "And once they have chosen to live in that arrangement, their status was raised higher than other women to the extent that one deed done by them was made to stand for two."

## One deed made to stand for two

**"Whoever of you commits an open fāḥishah, the torment for her will be doubled."** Ibn Kathir stresses that this is a conditional phrase and "does not imply that what is referred to would actually happen" — the Qur'an poses conditions of the same kind elsewhere (39:65, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself; 6:88; 43:81; 39:4). The framing is protective: "Because their status is so high, it is appropriate to state that the sin, if they were to commit it, would be so much worse, so as to protect them and their Hijab."

**What is fāḥishah here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the word is used both for acts of shame and for disobedience and sin generally — and the first is ruled out here, because Allah has kept the wives of all His prophets immune from that serious fault. The word **mubayyinah** ("open, clear, manifest") supports this: acts of shamelessness are precisely what is *not* manifest — they take place secretly. So fāḥishah *mubayyinah* here means common sins, or the causing of pain to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means *nushūz* — rebellion — "and a bad attitude." Muqātil ibn Sulaymān said the sense is either disobeying the Prophet ﷺ or demanding of him something whose fulfilment is hard on him (reported by al-Bayhaqī in *As-Sunan*). Mālik narrated from Zayd bin Aslam that the doubling means "in this world and the next"; something similar was narrated from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid.

**The other side of the scale.** Here, Ibn Kathir observes, "Allah mentions His justice and His bounty." Ayah 31 promises the reward twice over to whoever among them **stays obedient (yaqnut) and acts righteously**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes an asymmetry: the doubled punishment is tied to one thing only, the doubled reward to two conditions. "The reason is that reward comes only when obedience is perfect while, for punishment, even a single sin is enough."

**Why doubled at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two reasons. First, the verse is "in a way a recompense" for what the blessed wives did at the revelation of the Verse of Choice, when they chose to remain wedded to the Prophet ﷺ and sacrificed whatever material benefits lay in doing otherwise. Second, the doubled punishment arises from the same eminence — from "their special superiority and distinctive gentleness," and because "Divine punishment for heedlessness and rebellion does increase in proportion to the honor and regard in which one is held."

**The noble provision.** Ibn Kathir understands this as Paradise — the dwellings of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the highest reaches of ʿIlliyyīn, in al-Wasīlah, the closest of the dwellings of Paradise to the Throne.

**Not sealed off from the rest of us.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this distinction does not mean no one else may be blessed with a two-fold reward — the Qur'an says of those from the People of the Book who embraced Islam, "Such people will be given their reward twice" (28:54). Imām Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ said in *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān* that the reason for the doubling — their being the special recipients of prophetic knowledge and divine revelation — is present also in the ʿulamāʼ: a scholar whose practice accords with his knowledge finds the reward of that deed greater than others', and if he commits some sin, the punishment too is greater.

## Five instructions, and who is bound by them

**"O wives of the Prophet! You are not like any other women"** — Ibn Kathir reads this as telling them to fear Allah as He commanded, and that no other woman is their equal in virtue and status. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts what follows, across ayah 32 and ayah 33, as five instructions: two concerning speech and hijab, then prayer, zakāh, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger.

But the precedence is at once qualified: **"if you have taqwā."** Qurṭubī and Mazharī, as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, read the condition as a caution against relying on the relationship itself; the superiority rests instead on their observing taqwā and obeying Allah's injunctions.

Does this make them superior to all the women of the world? Against that stands the verse about Maryam — "Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you over the women of all the worlds" (3:42) — and the hadith of Anas in Tirmidhī, in which the Prophet ﷺ named four as sufficient to hold in esteem among all women: Maryam daughter of ʿImrān, Khadījah daughter of Khuwaylid, Fāṭimah daughter of Muhammad ﷺ, and Āsiyah the wife of Pharaoh. So the precedence in ayah 32 belongs to their particular standing as the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and does not establish an absolute superiority running counter to other texts (Mazharī).

**The first instruction: "Then be not soft in speech."** As-Suddī and others explained this as not being gentle in speech when addressing men. Ibn Zayd glossed the corrective, "speak in an honorable manner," as "decent and honorable talk that is known to be good" — which, Ibn Kathir explains, means a woman should not address a non-maḥram man as she addresses her husband. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that even where a non-maḥram must be spoken to from behind a screen, the softness of tone that might stir an inclination in the listener's heart should still be avoided.

**"Lest he in whose heart is a disease should be moved with desire."** The desire meant, Ibn Kathir says, is something unclean. Mazharī opens up "disease": it means hypocrisy, or its offshoots. A sincere believer who inclines towards something unlawful is no hypocrite yet is certainly weak in faith — and that weakness is itself an offshoot of hypocrisy, since with faith pure and free of the least element of it, no one can ever tilt towards the ḥarām.

Some of the Mothers of the Believers took this so much to heart that, when speaking to a non-maḥram man, they would put a hand over the mouth so that the voice would change. From the verse Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a ruling: **a woman's voice is not itself included under *satr*** — what must be concealed — but a precautionary restriction is placed on its manner.

**The second instruction: "And stay in your houses."** Ibn Kathir: stay in your houses and do not come out except for a purpose — and one purpose mentioned in the Sharīʿah is prayer in the masjid, so long as the conditions are fulfilled, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the masjids of Allah, but have them go out without wearing fragrance" — and according to another report, "even though their houses are better for them."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works out how far the command reaches. It establishes *al-ḥijāb bil-buyūt* — the home itself serving as the veil. Yet the next clause, "do not display yourselves," indicates that going out as needed is not prohibited absolutely; what is prohibited is going out displaying adornment. Ayah 59 of this surah, telling believing women to "bring down over themselves part of their outer garments," itself shows that women have permission to go out — on condition that they go out covered. And the Prophet ﷺ clarified that occasions of need are exempt, saying to his wives, "You are permitted to go out for your needs" (reported by Muslim). His practice after the verse of hijab confirms it: his wives went with him for Hajj and ʿUmrah on sound and authentic reports, and with him in many battles. After his passing they went for Hajj and ʿUmrah too, except Sawdah and Zaynab bint Jaḥsh — whose abstention, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, rested not on this verse but on their reading of a hadith spoken after the Farewell Hajj, which the other wives, including a jurist of the rank of ʿĀʼishah, understood to permit journeys for a recognised act of worship. ʿUmar himself sent them for Hajj, sending ʿUthmān and ʿAbd ur-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf to manage it.

The exemptions thus cover Hajj and ʿUmrah, duties owed to parents, visiting maḥram relatives in health and sickness; and a woman with no arrangement for her living expenses may go out in hijab to earn an honourable living — always without display of adornment, covered with burqaʿ or jilbāb.

**Tabarruj.** The word means manifestation or display; here, the display of personal adornment before non-maḥram men, as in "not displaying embellishment" (24:60). Mujāhid: "Women used to go out walking in front of men, and this was the tabarruj of Jāhiliyyah." Qatādah: when they go out of their homes "walking in a shameless and flirtatious manner." Muqātil bin Ḥayyān: "Tabarruj is when a woman puts a khimār on her head but does not tie it properly," so that her necklaces, earrings and neck can be seen. Ibn Kathir adds that on tabarruj Allah addresses all the women of the believers. And in **"the *first* Jāhiliyyah,"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds a hint that a later age of ignorance would come in which a similar display of immodesty becomes rampant.

**The third, fourth and fifth instructions: "And establish the prayer, and give zakāh, and obey Allah and His Messenger."** Ibn Kathir notes the order: Allah first forbids them from evil, then enjoins good — prayer, which means worshipping Allah alone with no partner, and zakāh, which means doing good to other people — then closes with obedience to Allah and His Messenger, "an instance of something specific being followed by something general."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks what ayah 32's opening raises: if these women "are not like any other women," are these rulings theirs alone? Nobody could imagine that prayer, zakāh and obedience are peculiar to the blessed wives — and on reflection the two hijab-related instructions are not either; the same injunctions apply to all Muslim women. The speciality lies not in the rulings but in the care owed in keeping them: "the blessed wives are not like common women, because the state of their dignity is the highest of all."

## The household Allah intends to keep pure

**"Allah only intends to keep filth away from you, O people of the House, and to make you pure through a perfect purification."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as the reason for the special address: through this instruction in the bettering of deeds, Allah intends to bless the household of His Messenger ﷺ with an ideal purity, removing everything counter to it.

**Ar-rijs.** The word carries several senses in the Qur'an: idols ("So refrain from the filth of idols," 22:30), sin in absolute terms, and at times punishment, or impurity, or filth. The outcome, per *Al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ*, is that everything legally or naturally detestable is rijs, and here the word appears in that general sense.

**Who are the Ahl al-Bayt?** Ibn Kathir treats the wives' inclusion as beyond doubt: the ayah is "a clear statement that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ are included among the members of his family," and "the scholars are unanimously agreed that they were the reason for revelation in this case." Ibn Jarīr recorded that ʿIkrimah used to call the verse out in the marketplace, saying it was revealed solely concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and offering a mubāhalah — the mutual invoking of Allah's curse — to whoever disagreed. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Ibn ʿAbbās to the same effect, citing ayah 34 — "what is recited in *your* houses," in the feminine — as his proof (reported from him by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr). Ibn Kathir concludes that they alone were the reason for revelation, "but others may be included by way of generalization."

Alongside this stands the hadith of the cloak. ʿĀʼishah related that the Prophet ﷺ went out one morning wearing a striped cloak of black camel's hair; al-Ḥasan came and he wrapped him in it with him, then al-Ḥusayn, then Fāṭimah, then ʿAlī, and then he recited this ayah — recorded by Muslim; and in a narration reported by Ibn Jarīr he added, "O Allah, these are the members of my family." In his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, Muslim also records Zayd ibn Arqam's account of the address by the well of Khumm, where the Prophet ﷺ said three times, "Remember Allah with regard to the members of my family." Asked whether his wives counted, Zayd answered that they are members of his family, but that the members of his family are those not permitted to receive charity after his death — the families of ʿAlī, ʿAqīl, Jaʿfar and ʿAbbās. Ibn Kathir notes of this last part: "This commentary is from Zayd bin Arqam and is not marfūʿ."

Ibn Kathir's resolution, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows, is that there is no contradiction: that the verse was revealed concerning the high station of the blessed wives does not exclude others. So the blessed wives are included in any case, being the direct addressees — and Fāṭimah, ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn too, on the strength of the Prophet's ﷺ own statement. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a grammatical argument: throughout this stretch the address is feminine, yet in this one clause the pronouns switch to the masculine, *ʿankum* and *yuṭahhirakum* — strong evidence that men are included among those addressed.

**What purification is meant?** Through these instructions, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, Allah will keep the Ahl al-Bayt protected against satanic instigations, sins and evils, and make them pure. What is meant is *tashrīʿī* — legal — purification, not the *takwīnī*, creational, purification which is the hallmark of the prophets; it does not follow that they are all *maʿṣūm*, protected such that sin is not even possible. Some have gone further, treating *tathīr* here as establishing *ʿiṣmah* and excluding the wives from the term altogether; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's author answers this at length in his *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān* on this surah, showing on legal proofs that ʿiṣmah is restricted to the prophets and the angels.

## The blessing named at the end

**"And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah and the wisdom."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two senses of *udhkurna*: to be mindful of these verses and points of wisdom personally, which should issue in acting on them; and to pass on to the Muslim community whatever of the Qur'an was revealed in their homes and whatever teachings of the Prophet ﷺ they received. *Āyāt Allāh* means the Qur'an, and *al-ḥikmah*, as the commentators at large have explained, the teachings and Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir reports the command as: act in accordance with that of the Qur'an and Sunnah which Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ in your houses — the view of Qatādah and others — and remember this blessing with which you alone of all people have been favoured. Qatādah's own comment was that in it "He is reminding them of His favour." Ibn Kathir singles out ʿĀʼishah as foremost in this blessing, since the revelation did not come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the bed of any of his wives except hers, as he ﷺ stated.

From this ayah Ibn al-ʿArabī drew a general obligation in his *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān*: whoever hears a verse of the Qur'an, or a statement of hadith, is duty-bound to convey it to the Muslim ummah — so much so that even the blessed wives were bound to convey what was revealed in their homes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the point: because *ḥikmah* here means the Sunnah, the spreading and teaching of the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ is made necessary in the same way as that of the Qur'an. The *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī relates the incident of Muʿādh, who heard a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ but did not narrate it publicly, fearing people might not give it the status it deserved; yet when death approached he gathered people and narrated it, saying the time had come to deliver back to its real owner, the Muslim ummah, what had been held in trust.

**"Indeed, Allah is Laṭīf, Khabīr."** Ibn Kathir: by His kindness towards you, you have reached this status, and by His knowledge that you are qualified for it, He has given it to you and singled you out for it. And ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī on the two names: "He knows when and where to reveal al-Ḥikmah."

## What the passage asks of us

Ibn Kathir frames these commands as "the good manners which Allah enjoined upon the wives of the Prophet ﷺ so that they would be an example for the women of the Ummah to follow." Three things carry over: proportion — the closer one stands to the knowledge of the dīn, the more one's deeds weigh in both directions; the asymmetry of ayah 31, a warning against resting on status instead of taqwā, the condition ayah 32 attaches to it; and the duty of ayah 34, that what one has received of Allah's verses and the Prophet's ﷺ wisdom is a trust to be lived and handed on.

passages.title: The ten pairs of righteous men and women
passages.tafsir:
This single ayah answers a question a woman put to the Prophet ﷺ: why does the Qur'an seem to speak of men? Allah replies not with a sentence but with a roll-call — ten qualities, each one named twice, once in the masculine and once in the feminine — and then a single promise for all of them together: forgiveness and a great reward. What holds the ayah together is that repeated pairing.

## The question behind the revelation

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, that she said to him: "Why is it that we are not mentioned in the Qur'an as men are?" She then describes the answer arriving. She was combing her hair when she heard him calling from the minbar; she tied her hair back, went out to her chamber, and listened — and he ﷺ was saying from the minbar: *"O people! Verily Allah says: 'Verily, the Muslims: men and women, the believers: men and women…'"* to the end of the ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that An-Nasa'i and Ibn Jarir also recorded it.

Notice how the answer came: not as a private reply to one wife, but from the minbar, opening with *O people*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers more of this. It cites narrations in which women said to the Prophet ﷺ, in substance: we see Allah mentioning men everywhere in the Qur'an and addressing them, as though there is almost no good in us; we are afraid our own worship may not even be accepted. Maʿārif attributes such a report to al-Baghawi from the blessed wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and notes similar submissions from Umm ʿUmarah al-Ansariyyah, may Allah be pleased with her — which appear in Tirmidhi with the authority rating *hasan* (good) — and from Asma' bint ʿUmays, may Allah be pleased with her. In all these narrations, Maʿārif says, this very submission is identified as the cause of the ayah's revelation.

That is a striking thing to sit with. The concern reported here was not a demand for status; it was a fear about acceptance. *Is my worship even being counted?* And the Qur'an answers by naming the women ten times over.

## Why the Qur'an usually addresses men — and what that does and does not mean

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here to explain the Qur'anic style that prompted the question. In its usual injunctions, both men and women are addressees, but generally the address is made to men, with women included as a corollary. Maʿārif reads a hint in this: that all matters relating to women are shielded, concealed and curtained, and that in this there is honour and esteem for them.

Maʿārif then points to something remarkable. Ponder the whole Qur'an, it says, and you will find that no woman is referred to by her personal name except Maryam bint ʿImran (peace be upon her). Elsewhere women are mentioned under the cover of their attribution to men — *the wife of Pharaoh*, *the wife of Nuh*, *the wife of Lut*. Maryam may be the exception, Maʿārif suggests, because ʿIsa (peace be upon him) could not be attributed to any father, so the attribution had to run through the mother; it was for that attribution that her name was disclosed. Maʿārif ends the point, as scholars do with what cannot be settled, with *and Allah knows best*.

But wisdom in a style does not cancel a heart's discomfort with it. Maʿārif says plainly that it was natural for women to feel some sort of discomfort about it, and that in these verses special mention was made of the acceptability of their deeds *to mollify the hearts of women*. And it states the principle the ayah makes clear: the touchstone of acceptance and appreciation with Allah is the righteousness of deeds and the spirit of obedience to Him, and in this there is no discrimination between man and woman.

## The ten pairs, one by one

The ayah does not simply say "believing men and women." It builds a portrait, quality by quality. Ibn Kathir walks through each.

**1–2. Muslim men and women; believing men and women.** Ibn Kathir takes the fact that Allah names both *islām* and *īmān* as an indication that *īmān* (faith) is something other than *islām*, and more specific than it. His proof is Allah's word about the bedouins: *"The bedouins say: 'We believe.' Say: 'You believe not, but you only say, We have surrendered (in Islam), for faith has not yet entered your hearts'"* (49:14). *Islām* here is the outward surrender; *īmān* is what has entered the heart.

He adds a second proof from the Two Sahihs: *"The adulterer does not commit adultery at the time when he is a believer."* Sin, he explains, snatches away a person's *īmān* — yet, by the consensus of the Muslims, that does not mean he is a disbeliever. That careful sentence is important creed: naming this level does not turn major sin into apostasy. It shows that *īmān* is more specific than bare *islām*.

**3. The *qānit* men and women.** Ibn Kathir defines *qunūt* as obedience during quiet time. He lets the Qur'an fill the word out: *"Is one who is qānit, prostrating himself or standing in the middle of the night, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord…"* (39:9); *"All are qānitūn to Him"* (30:26); *"O Maryam! Be devoutly obedient to your Lord and prostrate, and bow with those who bow"* (3:43); *"And stand before Allah qānitīn"* (2:238). From these he draws a conclusion about these first three qualities: beyond Islam there is a higher level to be reached, which is *īmān* — and *qunūt* stems from them both.

**4. The truthful men and women.** This refers to their speech, says Ibn Kathir, for truthfulness is a praiseworthy attribute. He notes that some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were never known to have lied even once — neither during the days of ignorance before Islam nor after it. Truthfulness is a sign of faith, just as lying is a sign of hypocrisy. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ teaching that truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise, while lying leads to immorality and immorality leads to the Fire — and that a man will keep telling the truth and striving to do so until he is recorded with Allah as truthful, just as a man will keep telling lies and persist in it until he is recorded with Allah as a liar. (Ibn Kathir gives this teaching without naming a collection here, adding that there are many hadiths on the topic.) The mechanism is worth noticing: a name with Allah is earned by persistence, not by a single act.

**5. The patient men and women.** Ibn Kathir describes this as the attribute of those who are steadfast: patience in the face of adversity, and knowing that what is decreed will inevitably come to pass, so that they face it with patience and steadfastness. Then a line of real pastoral realism: patience is most difficult when disaster first strikes, and after that it becomes easier — and this is true steadfastness.

**6. The *khāshiʿ* men and women.** *Khushūʿ*, he says, means serenity and tranquillity, deliberation, dignity and humility. And he names what motivates a person to be like this: fear of Allah and the awareness that He is constantly watching — as in the hadith, *"Worship Allah as if you can see Him, for if you cannot see Him, He can see you."* (Ibn Kathir cites it here without naming a collection.) Note the direction of travel: *khushūʿ* is not a mood manufactured for the moment of prayer; it is what the awareness of being seen does to a person's bearing.

**7. The men and women who give charity.** *Ṣadaqah*, Ibn Kathir explains, means doing good to people who are in need or who are weak and have no means of earning a living and none to support them; the givers give from the excess of their wealth in obedience to Allah and as a good deed to His creation. From the Two Sahihs he cites the seven whom Allah will shade with His shade on the Day when there is no shade except His — among them a man who gave in charity and concealed it to the extent that his left hand did not know what his right hand was giving. And according to another hadith: *"Ṣadaqah extinguishes bad deeds just as water extinguishes fire."*

**8. The fasting men and women.** Ibn Kathir cites a hadith narrated by Ibn Majah: *"Fasting is the zakah of the body"* — in other words, it purifies the body and cleanses it of things that are bad in both physical and Shariʿah terms.
