He records Saʿid bin Jubayr's saying that whoever fasts Ramadan and three days of each month is included in this phrase of the ayah. And he notes that fasting is one of the greatest means of overcoming one's desires, quoting the Prophet's ﷺ counsel to young men: whoever among them can afford to marry should marry, for it is most effective in lowering the gaze and protecting chastity, and whoever cannot should fast, for it will be a protection for him.

**9. The men and women who guard their chastity.** Ibn Kathir says it is quite apt that this should be mentioned next — fasting was just named as the protection, and now comes what is being protected. The meaning is that they protect themselves from forbidden and sinful things, except for what is permitted, as Allah says: *"And those who guard their chastity, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess — for they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors"* (70:29–31).

**10. The men and women who remember Allah much.** This is remembrance with the hearts and the tongues both. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abi Hatim, from Abu Saʿid Al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said that if a man wakes his wife at night and the two of them pray two rakʿahs, they will be recorded that night among the men and the women who remember Allah much — recorded also, Ibn Kathir notes, by Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Abu Saʿid and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both. Worth pausing over: the description is earned here by a husband and wife together, at night, in two rakʿahs.

He also records from Imam Ahmad, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ was walking along a road in Makkah and came to the mountain of Jumdan and said: "This is Jumdan; go ahead, for the *mufarridūn* have gone ahead." They asked who the *mufarridūn* were, and he ﷺ said: *"The men and the women who remember Allah much."* Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim also recorded it, except for the last part of it. The picture is of travellers on a road with some already far ahead — and the ones out in front are simply those who remember Allah much.

## Why *this* act is the one commanded "much"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to walk past. Islam, it says, stands on five acts of worship — Salah, Zakah, fasting, Hajj and Jihad — yet there is no injunction in the entire Qur'an commanding any one of these to be done *abundantly*. (That enumeration is Maʿārif's own wording; the point it is pressing concerns the command to do something abundantly, not a re-listing of the pillars.) The remembrance of Allah, by heart or tongue, is ordered abundantly in several places, including Surah Al-Anfal (8:45), Surah Al-Jumuʿah (62:10), and here in this ayah.

Why? Maʿārif gives two reasons.

First, dhikr is the essential spirit of all acts of worship. It cites a narration of Muʿadh Ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: someone asked the Prophet ﷺ which of the fighters deserves the best of returns, and he ﷺ said, the one who makes the dhikr of Allah most abundantly; and which of the fasting people is most reward-worthy — the one who makes the dhikr of Allah most abundantly; and similar questions were asked about Salah, Zakah, Hajj and charity, and every time the answer was the same. (Maʿārif attributes the report to Ahmad, via Ibn Kathir.) In other words, dhikr is not merely one more item on the list of ten; it is what the other acts of worship carry within them.

Second, it is the easiest of all acts of worship, and the Shariʿah has placed no condition on it: with wudu' or without, lying down, sitting, or walking, at all times. It demands no hard labour and no formal free time. And yet, Maʿārif says, so great is its effect that even worldly chores transform into worship through it. This is why the Prophet ﷺ taught prayers for before and after eating, for going out and coming back, for before travel, during it and on returning home, and before and after starting a business. The outcome of that whole treasure of prophetic prayers is that no Muslim should do anything at any time while heedless of Allah — and if a person makes these part of the fabric of daily work, then *dunya becomes deen*: worldly duties begin to release the fragrance of faith.

## Living it

Ten qualities — outward submission, inward faith, quiet obedience, honest speech, endurance under blows, humility before the One who sees, open-handedness, discipline of the body, guarded chastity, and a tongue and heart that keep returning to Allah — and every one of them named for men and for women alike. Any believer reading the list can find the one that is thinnest in them and start there.

And the ayah closes by handing all ten the same promise: *"Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward."* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us that for all of those mentioned in this ayah, He has prepared forgiveness of their sins and a great reward — meaning Paradise. Note the verb *prepared*: it is already done, waiting. Forgiveness of sins comes first, and then a reward that Allah describes simply as *great*.

The woman who asked whether her worship was being counted received an answer that has been recited in every generation since. Her question was honoured, not deflected — and the shape of the answer speaks for itself: ten times over, no one left out.
